blocks.title: Radiant flux intensity
blocks.text: Radiant flux intensity is the amount of electromagnetic energy per unit area per unit time emitted from a star that reaches the Earth's surface.

blocks.title: Tidbit!
blocks.text: If Earth were twice as far from the Sun, the sunlight reaching it would be only one-fourth as intense. Such low energy might have made the evolution of life impossible.

It is a small fraction of the total value of luminosity. In other words, radiant flux intensity is the luminosity per unit area measured on the surface of Earth. Radiant flux intensity from a star at a distance d is expressed as:

items: Two stars appear equally bright in the night sky. However, one is 10 times farther away than the other. Which star is more luminous, and by how much?

blocks.text: where L is the luminosity and 4πr² is the surface area of star. As the luminosity of a star remains constant, therefore, radiant flux intensity follows inverse square law with distance as demonstrated in Fig. 21.1. According to this law, when the distance from centre of a star is doubled (from r to 2r), intensity of the radiant flux reduces to one-fourth of its original value. Similarly, increasing the distance to three times its initial length (3r), decreases the flux by a factor of nine, and this pattern continues accordingly.
book_errors: 4πr² is the surface area of star

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book calls 4πr² "the surface area of star". In F = L/4πr², r is the distance from the star to the place where the flux is measured (the distance d of the sentence before), so 4πr² is the area of an imaginary sphere of that radius over which the star's luminosity spreads, not the surface area of the star itself.

blocks.alt: A point source on the left with straight lines spreading from it. At distance r the lines pass the edges of one square; at 2r the same lines enclose a square made of four such squares; at 3r a square of nine squares. Marks below show the distances r, 2r and 3r from the source.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.1: Schematic illustration of the inverse-square law for radiant flux intensity (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.1).

blocks.title: Example 21.2
blocks.problem: The luminosity of a star is 4.50 ×10²⁶ W. It is located at a distance of 1.40 × 10¹¹ m from a planet. Calculate the radiant flux intensity of the star at the surface of that planet.
